svg.title: 04b · High Availability, Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery: Target
svg.desc: Proposed design. FSP traffic reaches the active primary site through global load balancing or DNS failover. The primary site spreads services and stateful members across three zones with synchronous database replication. A warm-standby DR site receives asynchronous replication, the same GitOps release and replicated secrets; backups go to a third location. Seven scenario cards describe detection, automatic response, impact and data loss. RPO and RTO are marked as design decisions.
svg.text: 04b · High Availability, Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery: Target
A proposed design: active primary site across three zones, warm-standby DR site, replicated data, tested runbooks. RPO and RTO are decisions, not facts.

SCENARIOS (TARGET BEHAVIOUR, TO BE PROVEN BY CHAOS AND DR TESTS)
Detect: All replicas healthy in 3 zones; DR site in
Respond: Synthetic transfers and alerts green
Detect: Pod crash or failed probe
Respond: Kubernetes restarts it; other replicas
Respond: Pods rescheduled; PDBs keep minimum
Respond: Automatic failover to a synchronous
Impact: Brief write pause; some in-flight transfers
Respond: Leader election; RF 3 keeps the data
Detect: Site monitoring, failed synthetic transfers
Respond: DR runbook: freeze, promote DR DB, scale
switch-back in a window; reconcile with FSPs
Committed in the replicated database → final; FSPs confirm with GET /transfers/{id}
Reserved but not committed → expires after failover (3303); reserved funds are released
Not recorded (lost in Kafka or the replication gap) → GET returns 3208; the payer FSP treats it as failed
Then every FSP reconciles by transferId, and the hub operator reconciles positions before the next settlement window closes
Proposed design. The repository has no HA or DR configuration (see 04a). Validate with chaos tests and timed DR exercises, then record RPO and RTO.
